RSA lab: manual test walkthrough

A step-by-step play-through for the owner, to judge what the automated tester can't: whether each hint gets a stuck student moving, whether the sheet reads well, and whether the lab fits one teaching week. The tester (rsa_lab_test.py) has already confirmed that every command below works and that every bot reply quoted here appears. Allow 60 to 90 minutes.

On the desktop VM you have three pages, all served by the hackerbot_server:

  • Hackerbot's chat: http://hackerbot:8080/
  • this walkthrough: http://hackerbot:8080/manual_test.html (copy buttons, ticks saved in the browser)
  • the lab sheet as students will see it: http://hackerbot:8080/lab_sheet.html

Read each section of the lab sheet before its challenges: the walkthrough checks the sheet as well as the bot. Where Hackerbot gives you a random value, the commands below ask for it with read -p; type it once. Run everything in one terminal, so the values you type stay set.

Setup

U=$(whoami); echo "You are $U"
python3 -c "import Cryptodome; print('pycryptodome', Cryptodome.__version__)"
openssl version
  • Expect your random username, pycryptodome 3.11.0 and OpenSSL 3.0.x.
  • Hackerbot answers hello and list (11 challenges)

Lab sheet: Purpose to RSA by hand

Read up to and including "RSA by hand, with Python", and paste the worked example into python3.

  • Expect: 161 132; a list starting [5, 7, 13, 17, 19,; 53 1; 37 then 67; 84, 104, 'T'; 7, 41; [7, 41, 54, 100, 151, 34, 140, 140, 119, 93]; The Hobbit.
  • the explanation of e and d is enough to do challenges 1-5 without help
  • the "two 140s" question makes the point about textbook RSA

Challenges 1-5: RSA by hand

For each: say goto N and ready, answer wrongly once, then correctly.

  • Expect after ready: Over to you., the question, Say "answer X".
  • Expect for a wrong answer: Incorrect (your answer)
  • Expect for the right answer: Correct, a flag, then the next challenge's prompt.

The sheet's Python is the student's route; these one-liners give you the answers to compare with.

# 1: choose e
read -p "p: " p; read -p "q: " q; read -p "candidates (as listed, with commas): " c
python3 -c "import math; phi=($p-1)*($q-1); print(*[e for e in [$c] if math.gcd(e, phi) == 1])"

# 2: find d
read -p "p: " p; read -p "q: " q; read -p "e: " e
python3 -c "print(pow($e, -1, ($p-1)*($q-1)))"

# 3: encrypt m
read -p "m: " m; read -p "e: " e; read -p "N: " n
python3 -c "print(pow($m, $e, $n))"

# 4: decrypt c (d not given)
read -p "c: " c; read -p "p: " p; read -p "q: " q; read -p "e: " e
python3 -c "print(pow($c, pow($e, -1, ($p-1)*($q-1)), $p*$q))"

# 5: decrypt the word
read -p "d: " d; read -p "N: " n; read -p "the ct numbers (spaces between): " ct
python3 -c "print(''.join(chr(pow(int(x), $d, $n)) for x in '$ct'.split()))"
  • #1: clear that you list only the valid candidates, smallest first?
  • #2 and #4: the sheet's pow(e, -1, phiN) is enough?
  • #5: the hint (type the numbers into a list, run the decryption loop) is enough?

Lab sheet: RSA with OpenSSL

Run the section's commands. The private key file should start -----BEGIN PRIVATE KEY-----.

Challenge 6: key pair

Say goto 6, then ready before making anything.

  • Expect: I can't find /home/<you>/challenge_6. Create it first (mkdir), then make your keys inside it.
  • hint clear?

Save the private key as key.pub by mistake, then say ready:

mkdir -p ~/challenge_6 && cd ~/challenge_6
openssl genrsa -out key.priv 2048
cp key.priv key.pub
  • Expect: key.pub isn't an RSA public key. Did you save the private key under that name by mistake?
  • hint clear?

Make a 1024-bit key instead of 2048, export its public key, and say ready:

cd ~/challenge_6 && openssl genrsa -out key.priv 1024 && openssl rsa -in key.priv -pubout -out key.pub
  • Expect: key.priv isn't a 2048-bit key. Make a new one with openssl genrsa -out key.priv 2048, then export key.pub from it again.
  • hint clear?

Make a 2048-bit key pair and say ready (expect Well done :) and a flag):

cd ~/challenge_6 && openssl genrsa -out key.priv 2048 && openssl rsa -in key.priv -pubout -out key.pub

Challenge 7: encrypt a message

Say goto 7. Make the key pair, then put the text in quotes by mistake, and say ready:

read -p "Text from Hackerbot: " T7
mkdir -p ~/challenge_7 && cd ~/challenge_7
openssl genrsa -out key.priv 2048 && openssl rsa -in key.priv -pubout -out key.pub
echo "\"$T7\"" > message.txt
openssl pkeyutl -encrypt -pubin -inkey key.pub -in message.txt -out message.enc
  • Expect: message.enc decrypts, but not to <text>. Put exactly that text (no quotes) in a file and encrypt the file.
  • hint clear?

Now the right text, but encrypted with challenge 6's public key; say ready:

cd ~/challenge_7 && echo "$T7" > message.txt
openssl pkeyutl -encrypt -pubin -inkey ~/challenge_6/key.pub -in message.txt -out message.enc
  • Expect: I couldn't decrypt message.enc with key.priv. Did you encrypt it with this directory's key.pub (and -pubin)?
  • hint clear?

Encrypt with this directory's key and say ready (expect a flag):

cd ~/challenge_7 && openssl pkeyutl -encrypt -pubin -inkey key.pub -in message.txt -out message.enc

Lab sheet: Digital signatures

Run the section's commands: the signature as hex and 256 iou.sig, Verified OK, then a verification failure after the edit.

  • the comments and the xxd step make it clear what the signature is

Challenge 8: sign

Say goto 8. Sign the text, then change message.txt, and say ready:

read -p "Text from Hackerbot: " T8
mkdir -p ~/challenge_8 && cp ~/challenge_6/key.priv ~/challenge_6/key.pub ~/challenge_8/ && cd ~/challenge_8
echo "$T8" > message.txt
openssl dgst -sha256 -sign key.priv -out message.sig message.txt
echo x >> message.txt
  • Expect: message.txt should contain exactly <text> (no quotes).
  • hint clear?

Put the text back, but sign it with challenge 7's private key by mistake, and say ready:

cd ~/challenge_8 && echo "$T8" > message.txt && openssl dgst -sha256 -sign ~/challenge_7/key.priv -out message.sig message.txt
  • Expect: The signature doesn't verify against key.pub. Did you sign message.txt after its final edit, with the private half of key.pub, using -sha256?
  • hint clear?

Sign with the right key and say ready (expect Signature verified. Well done :) and a flag):

cd ~/challenge_8 && openssl dgst -sha256 -sign key.priv -out message.sig message.txt

Lab sheet: Key exchange

Do the Diffie-Hellman worked example (8 19 2 2).

Challenge 9: Diffie-Hellman

Say goto 9 and ready, then:

read -p "p: " p; read -p "g: " g; read -p "a: " a; read -p "B: " B
python3 -c "print(pow($g, $a, $p), pow($B, $a, $p))"

Answer with the two numbers the wrong way round first (expect Incorrect), then answer A secret.

  • Expect: a flag, and challenge 10's prompt.
  • hint clear?
  • the "who are you talking to?" paragraph leads into chains of trust

Lab sheet: Chains of trust and eMudhra

Read Chains of trust and When a CA gets key generation wrong, then do What a key of 4 looks like, pasting into python3 as a student would.

  • Expect: cat emudhra4.pem matches the PEM on the sheet exactly; the priv: dump is 47 zero bytes then 04.
  • chains of trust is clear enough without a hands-on exercise
  • the exhibit lands: is it obvious how absurd the key is?

Challenge 10: brute-force a CA key

Say goto 10 and ready.

  • Expect: The certificates are in /home/<you>/emudhra_ca. Start counting. and the question.

Follow the sheet (extract the public key, paste the loop into python3; leave Python open for challenge 11). Answer with a wrong number first (expect Incorrect), then the right one.

  • Expect: :) That was one of eMudhra's real keys. Now use it to sign a certificate of your own. and a flag.
  • the brute force took only a second or two

Challenge 11: forge a certificate

Follow the sheet: save recovered.pem in Python, then run the forging commands, but give the wrong bank name at the Bank website: prompt. Say ready.

  • Expect: fake.crt isn't for <bank>. Make the certificate request with -subj "/CN=<bank>".
  • hint clear?

Make it self-signed instead of signed by the intermediate, then say ready:

cd ~/emudhra_ca
read -p "Bank website from Hackerbot: " BANK
openssl req -new -key fake.key -subj "/CN=$BANK" -out fake.csr
openssl x509 -req -in fake.csr -signkey fake.key -days 30 -out fake.crt
  • Expect: fake.crt doesn't chain up to the Lab Trust root. Sign it as the intermediate: -CA lab_trust_inter.crt with -CAkey recovered.pem (the key you brute-forced).
  • hint clear?

Run the sheet's forging commands with the right name, check fake.crt: OK, and say ready.

  • Expect: Every browser that trusts the Lab Trust root would accept that as <bank>. That is what the eMudhra keys made possible., a flag and That was the last challenge.
  • the point about forgery (and the man in the middle) is clear

Lab sheet: The response

  • the revocation-versus-blocking paragraph and question read well
  • "How secure is RSA today?" works as optional reading

The whole lab

  • 11 flags in total
  • the flow from "weak key" to "the fix" works as a story
  • fits one teaching week (how long did it take you?)
  • the "How secure is RSA today?" reading is the right length
  • nothing a student needs is missing from the sheet
